A urachal cyst occurs when only a local area of the allantois remains patent, forming a fluid-filled cavity that does not typically drain urine externally.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): When the lumen of the intraembryonic portion of the allantois persists, a urachal fistula may cause urine to drain from the umbilicus.

category: Describe the development of urinary bladder and urethra
statement: The phallic part of the urogenital sinus exhibits sexual dimorphism. What physical movement does this segment undergo in relation to the growth of the genital tubercle?
options: It is pushed posteriorly toward the anal canal.
It migrates cranially to merge with the bladder neck.
It is pulled ventrally as the tubercle grows.
It remains stationary while the pelvic part descends.
It undergoes involution to form the vestibular glands.
correctOption: It is pulled ventrally as the tubercle grows.
optionExplanations: It is not pushed posteriorly; it is an anterior structure that moves further forward (ventrally).
Cranial migration is not observed; the shift is ventral and distal toward the external surface of the body wall.
Correct. As the genital tubercle (future penis or clitoris) expands, it exerts traction on the phallic part of the urogenital sinus, pulling it ventrally.
It is not stationary; its shape and position are actively modified by the growth of the external genitalia.
The phallic part does not involute; it forms the majority of the female vestibule and contributes to the male penile urethra.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 264 (Book Page): The last part is the phallic part of the urogenital sinus. It is flattened from side to side, and as the genital tubercle grows, this part of the sinus will be pulled ventrally.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: In a clinical comparison between different types of congenital polycystic kidney disease (PKD), which histological and developmental feature distinguishes Autosomal Recessive PKD (ARPKD) from Autosomal Dominant PKD (ADPKD)?
options: ADPKD results in renal failure during infancy, while ARPKD only manifests in late adulthood
ARPKD cysts form specifically from collecting ducts, whereas ADPKD cysts form from all segments of the nephron
ARPKD is caused by ureteric bud duplication, whereas ADPKD is caused by failure of nephron fusion
ADPKD is characterized by a complete absence of cilia, whereas ARPKD involves only ciliary overgrowth
ARPKD involves only the proximal convoluted tubules, while ADPKD involves only the glomeruli
correctOption: ARPKD cysts form specifically from collecting ducts, whereas ADPKD cysts form from all segments of the nephron
optionExplanations: This is inverted. ARPKD typically causes renal failure in infancy or childhood, whereas ADPKD usually does not cause renal failure until adulthood.
This is correct. The primary developmental difference noted is the segment of the renal unit where the cysts originate: collecting ducts for ARPKD and all nephron segments for ADPKD.
Ureteric bud duplication leads to duplicated ureters, not PKD. PKD is categorized as a ciliopathy related to ciliary function mutations.

Both ADPKD and ARPKD are linked to mutations in genes encoding proteins localized in the cilia (ciliopathies). They involve ciliary dysfunction rather than a simple 'absence' or 'overgrowth' contrast.
The text states that ARPKD involves the collecting ducts, and ADPKD involves all segments of the nephron. It is not limited to just proximal tubules or glomeruli.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 261 (Book Page): Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD)... is a progressive disorder in which cysts form from collecting ducts... In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), cysts form from all segments of the nephron.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
coreConcept: Embryological Origin of the Bladder Trigone
statement: The trigone of the urinary bladder undergoes a specific histological transition during development. Which statement correctly identifies the embryological origin and subsequent modification of this region?
options: It is derived from the allantois and remains endodermal throughout life.
It originates from endoderm and is later invaded by mesonephric mesoderm.
It is initially mesodermal and is later replaced by endodermal epithelium.
It arises from the phallic part of the urogenital sinus and becomes ectodermal.
It is formed by the fusion of the paramesonephric ducts and is purely mesodermal.
correctOption: It is initially mesodermal and is later replaced by endodermal epithelium.
optionExplanations: The majority of the bladder is derived from the urogenital sinus (endoderm), but the trigone specifically starts as mesoderm.
The trigone begins as mesoderm (from the mesonephric ducts) and is later replaced by endoderm, not the other way around.
Correct. The trigone is formed by the incorporation of the mesonephric ducts (mesoderm), but this lining is eventually replaced by the endodermal lining of the urogenital sinus.
The phallic part forms the lower urethra; the bladder and trigone are part of the upper urogenital sinus. The final lining is endodermal, not ectodermal.
Paramesonephric ducts form the uterus and tubes, not the bladder trigone.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 266 (Book Page): Because both the mesonephric ducts and ureters originate in the mesoderm, the mucosa of the bladder formed by incorporation of the ducts (the trigone of the bladder) is also mesodermal. With time, the mesodermal lining of the trigone is replaced by endodermal epithelium.

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
statement: Which of the following best describes the transition of the renal blood supply as the metanephros shifts from its pelvic origin to its definitive abdominal position?
options: Venous drainage is established first, which then guides the recruitment of arterial branches
The kidney is vascularized by successively higher aortic branches while lower vessels usually degenerate
The initial pelvic vessels elongate significantly to maintain supply throughout the ascent
A single pair of renal arteries follows the kidney upward from the pelvis to the abdomen
Internal iliac branches are replaced by superior mesenteric branches at the final stage
correctOption: The kidney is vascularized by successively higher aortic branches while lower vessels usually degenerate
optionExplanations: The sequence is primarily arterial-driven as described in embryology; the recruitment of arterial branches is dependent on the kidney's current level relative to the aorta.
Correct. The kidney receives blood from 'transient' aortic branches at progressively higher levels. Most lower vessels disappear, though some may persist as accessory arteries.
Embryonic renal vessels do not elongate; they are transient and are replaced by new sprouts from the aorta as the kidney reaches new levels.
There isn't a single pair of arteries that moves with the kidney; instead, a succession of different vessels forms and regresses.
The final renal supply comes from the aorta at the L2 level, not the superior mesenteric artery.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): During its ascent to the abdominal level, it is vascularized by arteries that originate from the aorta at continuously higher levels. The lower vessels usually degenerate, but some may remain.

category: Describe development of intermediate mesoderm and its derivatives
statement: A comparison between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesoderm reveals that they contribute to distinct portions of the definitive kidney. Which structure is derived specifically from the metanephric mesoderm?
options: Ureter
Renal pelvis
Collecting tubules
Distal convoluted tubule
Major and minor calyces
correctOption: Distal convoluted tubule
optionExplanations: The ureter is the proximal portion of the ureteric bud that connects the kidney to the bladder.
The renal pelvis is the initial dilated portion of the ureteric bud and is not derived from the metanephric mesoderm.
Collecting tubules are the distal-most components of the ureteric bud's branching generations, not part of the excretory unit (nephron).
The distal convoluted tubule, along with the proximal convoluted tubule and the loop of Henle, form the nephron (excretory unit), which develops from the metanephric mesoderm.
Major and minor calyces are components of the collecting system, which originates from the branching ureteric bud.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 260 (Book Page): Continuous lengthening of the excretory tubule results in formation of the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule (Fig. 16.6E,F). Hence, the kidney develops from two sources: (1) metanephric mesoderm, which provides excretory units; and (2) the ureteric bud, which gives rise to the collecting system.

category: Describe development of intermediate mesoderm and its derivatives
coreConcept: Dual Embryological Origin of the Metanephros
statement: The definitive kidney, or metanephros, arises from two distinct embryological sources derived from the intermediate mesoderm. Which of the following structures is specifically formed by the metanephric mesoderm?
options: Ureter
Collecting tubules
Proximal convoluted tubule
Major and minor calyces
Renal pelvis
correctOption: Proximal convoluted tubule
optionExplanations: The ureter is a derivative of the ureteric bud, which is an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct, not the metanephric mesoderm.
Collecting tubules are the distal-most part of the collecting system and are derived from the branching of the ureteric bud, not the metanephric mesoderm.
The metanephric mesoderm (blastema) forms the excretory units (nephrons). This includes the Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule.
The major and minor calyces arise from the first few generations of subdivisions of the ureteric bud as it branches into the metanephric blastema.
The renal pelvis is formed by the initial dilation of the ureteric bud after it penetrates the metanephric tissue cap.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 260 (Book Page): Hence, the kidney develops from two sources: (1) metanephric mesoderm, which provides excretory units; and (2) the ureteric bud, which gives rise to the collecting system. ... Continuous lengthening of the excretory tubule results in formation of the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule.

category: Describe development of intermediate mesoderm and its derivatives
statement: A 4-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic due to a palpable abdominal mass. Physical examination reveals aniridia (absence of iris). Genetic testing confirms a microdeletion on chromosome 11. Which embryological regulator is most likely disrupted, leading to the renal malignancy in this patient?
options: PAX2
SALL1
GDNF
WT1
EYA1
correctOption: WT1
optionExplanations: PAX2 mutations result in renal coloboma syndrome, characterized by renal hypoplasia and optic nerve defects, but not the malignancy described.
SALL1 mutations are responsible for Townes-Brock syndrome, which involves different malformations rather than Wilms tumor and aniridia.
GDNF is produced by the metanephric mesoderm to regulate ureteric bud branching; mutations cause renal agenesis, not Wilms tumor.
The child has WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, and Retardation). This is caused by a deletion on 11p13 involving WT1 (the tumor suppressor) and PAX6 (eye development).
EYA1 mutations are associated with branchiootorenal syndrome, which features ear anomalies and renal defects, not the combination of Wilms tumor and aniridia.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 261 (Book Page): Wilms tumor is due to mutations in the WT1 gene on 11p13... For example, WAGR syndrome is characterized by Wilms tumor, aniridia, gonadoblastomas... due to a microdeletion in chromosome 11 that includes both the PAX6 (aniridia) and WT1 genes.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A newborn is delivered via emergency cesarean section due to severe fetal distress. Physical examination reveals an exposed posterior bladder wall, widely spaced genital swellings, and an imperforate anus. The neonatologist suspects a severe ventral body wall defect. Which of the following conditions most likely explains this cluster of findings?
options: Isolated epispadias
Exstrophy of the cloaca
Bilateral renal agenesis
Urachal fistula
Exstrophy of the bladder
correctOption: Exstrophy of the cloaca
optionExplanations: Isolated epispadias involves an open urinary tract on the dorsal aspect of the penis but does not involve the anus or major body wall defects.

Exstrophy of the cloaca is the most severe form, involving failure of lateral fold closure and defective urorectal septum development, leading to the triad of exposed mucosa, widely spaced genitalia, and imperforate anus.
Bilateral renal agenesis would lead to Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, limb defects) but does not cause an externalized bladder or ventral wall opening.
A urachal fistula only involves a connection between the bladder and umbilicus without disrupting the ventral body wall or the anal canal.
Bladder exstrophy presents with exposed mucosa and epispadias, but unlike cloacal exstrophy, it does not typically involve the urorectal septum or result in an imperforate anus.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 266 (Book Page): Exstrophy of the cloaca (Fig. 16.16B) is a more severe ventral body wall defect... In addition to the closure defect, normal development of the urorectal septum is altered, such that anal canal malformations and imperforate anus occur. Furthermore... the genital swellings are widely spaced.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: The development of the metanephric excretory system requires a precise sequence of cellular inductions. Which structure is the direct precursor that differentiates into the S-shaped renal tubules under the influence of the collecting system?
options: Ureteric bud
Renal vesicles
Major calyces
Bowman capsule
Mesonephric duct
correctOption: Renal vesicles
optionExplanations: The ureteric bud is the inducer, not the precursor of the S-shaped tubules; it gives rise to the collecting system.
The renal vesicles are formed from the metanephric tissue cap and are the immediate precursors that elongate to form the S-shaped tubules of the nephron.
Major calyces are large drainage structures formed by the early branching of the ureteric bud, not microscopic precursors of nephrons.
Bowman capsule is a later stage of development, representing the proximal end of the S-shaped tubule after it is indented by a glomerulus.
The mesonephric duct is the source of the ureteric bud but does not differentiate into the excretory tubules of the permanent kidney.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 260 (Book Page): Under the inductive influence of the tubule, cells of the tissue cap form small vesicles, the renal vesicles, which in turn give rise to small S-shaped tubules.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: In cases of ureteral duplication, an ectopic ureter often results from the development of two ureteric buds. In a female patient, what is the most likely abnormal anatomical site for the ectopic ureter's orifice to be located?
options: The urachal sinus
The superior wall of the urinary bladder
The vagina, urethra, or vestibule
The rectum or anal canal
The uterine tube or ovary
correctOption: The vagina, urethra, or vestibule
optionExplanations: The urachal sinus is a remnant of the allantois at the apex of the bladder; ectopic ureters follow the path of the mesonephric duct toward the urethra/vagina.
The normal ureter enters the bladder at the trigone; the ectopic ureter moves down with the mesonephric duct to a lower, abnormal position.
Because the abnormal ureteric bud remains attached to the mesonephric duct as it migrates, it ends up in a lower position, frequently draining into the vagina, urethra, or vestibule in females.
The ureter is a derivative of the urogenital sinus, not the anal canal portion of the cloaca.
The mesonephric duct does not contribute to the uterine tubes or ovaries (which are paramesonephric/gonadal in origin).
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 262 (Book Page): In rare cases, one ureter opens into the bladder, and the other is ectopic, entering the vagina, urethra, or vestibule (Fig. 16.9C). This abnormality results from development of two ureteric buds.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A 3-year-old child presents with a renal mass, aniridia (absence of the iris), and intellectual disability. Which genetic abnormality is responsible for this constellation of symptoms?
options: Microdeletion in chromosome 11 (including PAX6 and WT1)
Duplication of the 11p13 region
Mutation in the cilia-related protein genes
Mutation in the SALL1 gene
Failure of the metanephric blastema to respond to GDNF
correctOption: Microdeletion in chromosome 11 (including PAX6 and WT1)
optionExplanations: The WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, Retardation) is caused by a contiguous gene deletion on chromosome 11p13, affecting both WT1 and PAX6.
The condition is caused by a microdeletion (loss of genetic material), not a duplication of the chromosome 11 region.
Cilia-related protein mutations cause ciliopathies like ADPKD or Bardet-Biedl syndrome, not the specific components of WAGR.
SALL1 mutations cause Townes-Brock syndrome, which involves limb and ear anomalies, but not the combination of Wilms tumor and aniridia.
Failure to respond to GDNF leads to renal agenesis, which results in the absence of a kidney, not a Wilms tumor mass.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 261 (Book Page): WAGR syndrome is characterized by Wilms tumor, aniridia, gonadoblastomas (tumors of the gonads), and mental retardation... The constellation of defects is due to a microdeletion in chromosome 11 that includes both the PAX6 (aniridia) and WT1 genes.

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
statement: At what stage of development does the definitive kidney (metanephros) typically begin its urine production, regardless of its final position?
options: 5th week
20th week
At birth
12th week
8th week
correctOption: 12th week
optionExplanations: The 5th week is when the metanephros first appears, but it is not yet functional.
The 20th week is well into the functional period; production starts much earlier.
Urine production must occur in utero to contribute to amniotic fluid volume; if it only started at birth, oligohydramnios would be the norm.
By the 12th week, the metanephros is functional and begins excreting urine into the amniotic fluid.
The 8th week marks the end of the embryonic period, but glomerular differentiation is not yet complete enough for urine production.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): The definitive kidney formed from the metanephros becomes functional near the 12th week. Urine is passed into the amniotic cavity and mixes with the amniotic fluid.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: A patient is found to have a kidney located at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae, with its ascent blocked by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Polycystic kidney disease
Horseshoe kidney
Wilms tumor
Pelvic kidney
Supernumerary kidney
correctOption: Horseshoe kidney
optionExplanations: Polycystic kidney disease involves the formation of numerous cysts and enlarged kidneys, but it does not involve fusion or mesenteric trapping.
In horseshoe kidney, the lower poles fuse; as they ascend, the isthmus becomes trapped under the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery.
Wilms tumor is a malignancy associated with WT1 mutations and presents as a mass, not a positional anomaly of a fused kidney.
A pelvic kidney remains near the common iliac artery but is not specifically described as being trapped by the inferior mesenteric artery.
A supernumerary kidney refers to an extra kidney, usually resulting from two ureteric buds, not a fusion of the lower poles during ascent.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 263 (Book Page): The horseshoe kidney is usually at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae because its ascent is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery (Fig. 16.11B).

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
coreConcept: Differential Anatomic Restriction of Renal Ascent
statement: Which anatomic landmark or structure differentiates the restriction of a pelvic kidney from the restriction observed in a horseshoe kidney?
options: A pelvic kidney is restricted by the pelvic brim, while a horseshoe kidney is restricted by the aortic bifurcation
A pelvic kidney is restricted by the urogenital ridge, while a horseshoe kidney is restricted by the adrenal glands
A pelvic kidney is trapped by the umbilical fork, while a horseshoe kidney is trapped by the inferior mesenteric artery
A pelvic kidney is trapped by the inferior mesenteric artery, while a horseshoe kidney is trapped by the umbilical fork
A pelvic kidney is trapped by the common iliac artery, while a horseshoe kidney is trapped by the urachus
correctOption: A pelvic kidney is trapped by the umbilical fork, while a horseshoe kidney is trapped by the inferior mesenteric artery
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The aortic bifurcation is near the origin of the umbilical arteries, but the specific landmark for the horseshoe kidney is the inferior mesenteric artery.

Incorrect. The urogenital ridge is a developmental site, not a mechanical barrier. The adrenal glands are the target destination for the kidneys, not a restricting factor in their ascent from the pelvis.

Correct. A pelvic kidney results when the organ fails to pass through the 'arterial fork' formed by the umbilical arteries. A horseshoe kidney ascends further but is halted by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery because its fused lower poles cannot pass over it.
Incorrect. This reverses the actual anatomical barriers; the IMA traps the fused horseshoe kidney, not the solitary pelvic kidney.

Incorrect. While a pelvic kidney is located near the common iliac, it is not trapped by it in the same sense as the umbilical fork. The urachus is related to the bladder, not the ascent of the kidney.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): Remaining in the pelvis close to the common iliac artery, it is known as a pelvic kidney (Fig. 16.11A)... The horseshoe kidney is usually at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae because its ascent is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: A 30-year-old patient is diagnosed with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD). Based on embryological pathology, how do the cysts in ADPKD differ from those found in the Autosomal Recessive form (ARPKD)?
options: ADPKD is caused by a complete lack of ureteric bud branching
ADPKD results in renal failure during early infancy
ADPKD cysts are localized only to the renal pelvis
Cysts in ADPKD develop from all segments of the nephron
Cysts in ADPKD only form in the collecting ducts
correctOption: Cysts in ADPKD develop from all segments of the nephron
optionExplanations: Failure of ureteric bud branching leads to renal agenesis or dysplasia (like multicystic dysplastic kidney), not the patterned cyst formation seen in ADPKD.
ADPKD typically presents with renal failure in adulthood, whereas ARPKD often causes failure in infancy or childhood.
The renal pelvis is generally spared from cyst formation; cysts are parenchymal and involve the microscopic tubular system.
The pathological hallmark of ADPKD is the development of cysts from any part of the nephron (PCT, loop, DCT) as well as collecting ducts, linked to ciliary protein mutations.
In ARPKD (recessive), cysts form primarily from the collecting ducts, whereas ADPKD involves all nephron segments.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 261 (Book Page): In autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), cysts form from all segments of the nephron and usually do not cause renal failure until adulthood. The autosomal dominant disease is more common... but less progressive than the autosomal recessive disease.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: Which developmental failure is primarily responsible for the occurrence of exstrophy of the bladder?
options: Over-secretion of the urachal lining
Failure of the metanephric mesoderm to migrate cranially
Malformation of the mesonephric duct
Failure of the lateral body wall folds to close in the midline pelvic region
Persistence of the primitive anal canal
correctOption: Failure of the lateral body wall folds to close in the midline pelvic region
optionExplanations: Over-secretion of the urachal lining leads to a urachal cyst, which is an internal pocket, not an external exposure of the entire bladder mucosa.
Metanephric mesoderm gives rise to the kidneys; its failure to migrate leads to pelvic kidneys, not exstrophy.
The mesonephric duct forms the collecting system and trigone; its malformation leads to renal or ureteral issues, not ventral body wall defects.
Bladder exstrophy is essentially a ventral body wall defect where the failure of lateral folds to fuse leaves the bladder mucosa exposed to the outside.
Persistence of the anal canal relates to hindgut malformations, not the exposure of the bladder through the abdominal wall.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): Exstrophy of the bladder (Fig. 16.16A) is a ventral body wall defect... probably due to failure of the lateral body wall folds to close in the midline in the pelvic region.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated for constant urinary dribbling despite normal voiding patterns. Imaging reveals a duplicated ureter on the right side. In females, if the abnormal ureteric bud has a low, ectopic entrance, which site is it most likely to enter?
options: Seminal vesicles
Vagina or vestibule
Prostatic urethra
Ejaculatory duct
Anal canal
correctOption: Vagina or vestibule
optionExplanations: Seminal vesicles are male-specific structures and can be sites for ectopic ureters in males.

In females, because the ectopic ureter follows the mesonephric duct's path or develops lower, it can drain into the vagina, vestibule, or urethra, causing bypass of the sphincter and constant dribbling.
The prostatic urethra is a site for ectopic ureters in males, not females.
The ejaculatory duct is a male structure formed from the mesonephric duct; it is not found in females.
The ureter is a derivative of the urinary system and does not enter the anal canal, which is a hindgut derivative.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 262 (Book Page): In rare cases, one ureter opens into the bladder, and the other is ectopic, entering the vagina, urethra, or vestibule (Fig. 16.9C).

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
statement: At approximately which week of development does the metanephros reach its definitive position and begin its excretory function?
options: 12th week
4th week
Birth
20th week
5th week
correctOption: 12th week
optionExplanations: Correct. By the 12th week, the kidney has largely completed its ascent and begins to produce urine, which is then passed into the amniotic cavity.
In the 4th week, the pronephros is forming and the mesonephros is just appearing; the metanephros has not yet formed.
Renal function must begin in utero to contribute to amniotic fluid volume; waiting until birth would result in Potter sequence due to oligohydramnios.
By the 20th week (end of the 5th month), collecting tubules are well developed, but function actually began much earlier at week 12.
The metanephros first appears in the 5th week, but it is still in the pelvis and not yet functional.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): The definitive kidney formed from the metanephros becomes functional near the 12th week.

category: Describe development of intermediate mesoderm and its derivatives
coreConcept: Embryogenesis of Renal Agenesis and Potter Sequence
statement: A newborn presents with severe respiratory distress, flattened facial features (Potter facies), and clubbed feet. Ultrasound reveals a complete absence of kidneys bilaterally. What is the primary embryological failure responsible for this sequence of clinical findings?
options: Lack of interaction between the metanephric mesoderm and the ureteric bud.
Persistence of the urachal lumen connecting the bladder to the umbilicus.
Failure of the urogenital ridge to form an ovoid organ during the second month.
Premature degeneration of the pronephric nephrotomes in the cervical region.
Mutation in the cilia-related proteins leading to cyst formation in collecting ducts.
correctOption: Lack of interaction between the metanephric mesoderm and the ureteric bud.
optionExplanations: Potter sequence results from oligohydramnios, which in this case is caused by bilateral renal agenesis due to the failed interaction (often regulated by GDNF/WT1) between the ureteric bud and metanephric mesoderm.
Persistence of the urachal lumen results in a urachal fistula, which causes urine drainage from the umbilicus but does not cause renal agenesis.
The urogenital ridge formation is a broad event; specific failure of kidney development is usually linked to the failure of ureteric bud induction of the metanephric blastema.
Pronephric degeneration is a normal developmental event and does not lead to renal agenesis or Potter sequence.
Ciliary mutations cause polycystic kidney disease, which may lead to renal failure but is a distinct pathology from complete agenesis.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 261 (Book Page): Renal agenesis may also arise if the interaction between the metanephric mesoderm and the ureteric bud fails to occur. ... Bilateral renal agenesis ... results in Potter sequence, characterized by anuria, oligohydramnios (decreased volume of amniotic fluid), and hypoplastic lungs secondary to the oligohydramnios.

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
coreConcept: Dynamic Vascular Adaptation of the Kidney
statement: As the metanephros undergoes its positional change from the pelvis to the abdominal level, how does its arterial vascularization dynamically adapt to this relocation?
options: The kidneys are vascularized only by the umbilical arteries until they reach the lumbar region
The kidney retains its original pelvic branch which becomes the definitive renal artery
The internal iliac artery provides new branches that sprout as the kidney ascends
Vascularization is provided by successive aortic branches at higher levels while lower vessels degenerate
The initial pelvic artery elongates and follows the kidney cranially
correctOption: Vascularization is provided by successive aortic branches at higher levels while lower vessels degenerate
optionExplanations: The umbilical arteries form a 'fork' that the kidneys pass through; they do not provide the primary vascular supply to the metanephros throughout its ascent.
The original pelvic branch is an embryonic vessel that usually disappears; retaining it as the only supply would be an anomaly, not the standard developmental process.
While the kidney is in the pelvis it receives supply from pelvic aortic branches, but its abdominal supply comes directly from the aorta, not the internal iliac system.
Correct. The kidney's ascent is marked by a sequential 'ladder-like' acquisition of higher aortic branches, with the simultaneous degeneration of more caudal vessels.
Renal arteries do not elongate from the pelvis; instead, new, higher-level arteries are formed while the older, lower ones are typically discarded.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): During its ascent to the abdominal level, it is vascularized by arteries that originate from the aorta at continuously higher levels. The lower vessels usually degenerate, but some may remain.

category: Describe the development of urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A neonate is born with an exposed bladder mucosa on the lower abdominal wall and a concomitant imperforate anus. Examination reveals that the genital swellings are widely spaced. What is the embryological basis for this specific constellation of defects?
options: Premature regression of the genital tubercle during the phallic stage
Isolated failure of the lateral body wall folds to close in the pelvic region
Persistence of the lumen of the intraembryonic portion of the allantois
Failure of the mesonephric ducts to incorporate into the bladder trigone
Disruption of both lateral body wall fold closure and normal development of the urorectal septum
correctOption: Disruption of both lateral body wall fold closure and normal development of the urorectal septum
optionExplanations: While the phallic part of the urogenital sinus is affected by the body fold failure, the primary cause of the described defects is the failure of closure and septation, not the regression of the tubercle itself.

Isolated failure of the lateral body wall folds to close typically results in exstrophy of the bladder. The addition of imperforate anus and widely spaced genital swellings indicates the more severe exstrophy of the cloaca.
Persistence of the allantoic lumen leads to urachal anomalies (fistulas, cysts, or sinuses) but does not result in the failure of the abdominal wall or the displacement of genital swellings.
Failure to incorporate mesonephric ducts would lead to ureteric ectopic openings or trigone abnormalities, not a major ventral body wall defect with an exposed bladder and anal malformations.

Exstrophy of the cloaca is characterized by a failure of lateral body wall closure combined with a failure of the urorectal septum to properly divide the cloaca, leading to both urogenital and anal defects.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): Exstrophy of the cloaca (Fig. 16.16B) is a more severe ventral body wall defect in which progression and closure of the lateral body wall folds are disrupted to a greater degree... In addition to the closure defect, normal development of the urorectal septum is altered, such that anal canal malformations and imperforate anus occur.

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
statement: What is the embryological origin of accessory renal arteries commonly found entering the superior or inferior poles of the definitive kidney?
options: Splitting of the main renal artery due to high blood pressure.
Compensatory branches from the gonadal arteries.
Hyperplastic branches of the suprarenal arteries.
Persistence of embryonic vessels that formed during the ascent of the kidneys.
New vascular sprouts induced by the adrenal gland.
correctOption: Persistence of embryonic vessels that formed during the ascent of the kidneys.
optionExplanations: Accessory arteries are developmental remnants, not the result of mechanical splitting or hemodynamic stress.
Gonadal arteries and renal arteries are distinct; while both arise from the aorta, one does not normally compensate for the other embryologically.
Suprarenal arteries have a distinct developmental path and do not typically form accessory renal poles.
During ascent, the kidney is supplied by successive aortic branches. If any of these lower transient vessels fail to degenerate, they remain as accessory renal arteries.
The adrenal glands have their own blood supply; they do not induce accessory renal vascularization.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): Accessory renal arteries are common; they derive from the persistence of embryonic vessels that formed during ascent of the kidneys.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A patient presents with a persistent anatomical remnant of the allantois that is closed at the umbilical end and the bladder end but remains patent in the middle, forming a fluid-filled cavity. How is this specific anomaly classified?
options: Exstrophy of the bladder
Urachal sinus
Exstrophy of the cloaca
Urachal fistula
Urachal cyst
correctOption: Urachal cyst
optionExplanations: Exstrophy of the bladder is a ventral body wall defect involving the failure of fold closure, not a persistence of the allantoic lumen.
A urachal sinus occurs when only the distal (upper) part of the allantoic lumen remains patent, typically opening onto the umbilicus but not connecting to the bladder.
Exstrophy of the cloaca is a more severe ventral wall defect involving the urorectal septum and anal canal, distinct from simple urachal remnants.
A urachal fistula represents a total patency of the allantois lumen, providing a direct communication (and urine drainage) from the bladder to the umbilicus.
A urachal cyst occurs when a localized middle segment of the allantois remains patent while the umbilical and vesical ends obliterate, forming a secluded secretory cavity.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): If only a local area of the allantois persists, secretory activity of its lining results in a cystic dilation, a urachal cyst.

category: Describe the development of urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A comparison between different urachal anomalies reveals distinct clinical presentations. Which of the following conditions is characterized by a persistent lumen in the superior part of the urachus that remains continuous with the urinary bladder?
options: Exstrophy of the bladder
Urachal cyst
Urachal sinus
Epispadias
Urachal fistula
correctOption: Urachal sinus
optionExplanations: Exstrophy of the bladder is a ventral body wall defect involving the failure of lateral body folds to close, exposing the bladder mucosa.
A urachal cyst occurs when a local, isolated area of the allantois persists and secretes fluid, but it does not maintain continuity with the bladder or the exterior.

A urachal sinus occurs when the distal (cranial) or upper portion of the allantois fails to close. While the quote mentions it is continuous with the bladder, clinical texts often specify the sinus opens to the umbilicus; however, per the source provided, the 'upper part' persistence forms the sinus continuous with the bladder.
Epispadias is a urethral defect where the opening is on the dorsal surface of the penis, often associated with bladder exstrophy.
A urachal fistula represents a total failure of allantoic obliteration, resulting in a direct communication between the bladder and the umbilicus, leading to urine drainage.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): When the lumen in the upper part persists, it forms a urachal sinus. This sinus is usually continuous with the urinary bladder.

category: List and describe the common congenital anomalies of kidney, urinary bladder and urethra
statement: Meckel-Gruber syndrome is a rare condition classified as a 'ciliopathy.' Which combination of clinical features must be present to suggest this specific diagnosis?
options: Anuria, oligohydramnios, and hypoplastic lungs
Bilateral renal agenesis and absence of the vagina
Renal cysts, hydrocephalus, and polydactyly
Wilms tumor, aniridia, and intellectual disability
Urachal cyst, epispadias, and imperforate anus
correctOption: Renal cysts, hydrocephalus, and polydactyly
optionExplanations: Option C is incorrect because these are the components of the Potter sequence.
Option E is incorrect because bilateral renal agenesis is a separate entity from the cystic manifestations of ciliopathies like Meckel-Gruber.

Option A is correct because the diagnostic triad for Meckel-Gruber syndrome typically includes renal cystic dysplasia, central nervous system malformations (like hydrocephalus or encephalocele), and post-axial polydactyly.
Option B is incorrect because these are the clinical components of WAGR syndrome.
Option D is incorrect because these are unrelated malformations from different embryological sites (allantois vs. body wall vs. cloaca).
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 262 (Book Page): Meckel-Gruber syndrome, characterized by renal cysts, hydrocephalus, microphthalmia, cleft palate, absence of the olfactory tract, and polydactyly.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: Which anatomical structure prevents the further cranial ascent of a 'horseshoe kidney', keeping it trapped at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae?
options: Common iliac artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Umbilical arteries
Celiac trunk
Inferior mesenteric artery
correctOption: Inferior mesenteric artery
optionExplanations: The common iliac artery is located at the site where a pelvic kidney might remain, but it is the inferior mesenteric artery that specifically traps the isthmus of a horseshoe kidney.
The superior mesenteric artery is located higher on the aorta and does not typically interfere with the ascent of a horseshoe kidney.
The umbilical arteries form the 'arterial fork' through which the kidneys normally pass; while they may cause the initial crowding that leads to fusion, they do not block the final ascent.
The celiac trunk is much more cranial than the typical resting position of a horseshoe kidney.
In a horseshoe kidney, the fused lower poles must cross the midline. As the kidney ascends, this bridge (isthmus) gets caught under the root of the inferior mesenteric artery.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): The horseshoe kidney is usually at the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae because its ascent is prevented by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery (Fig. 16.11B).

category: Describe the development of urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A clinician identifies a cystic dilation in the midline between the umbilicus and the bladder in a 2-year-old child. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this 'urachal cyst'?
options: Persistence of a localized area of the allantois with secretory activity
Failure of the lateral body wall folds to close
Persistence of only the upper part of the allantois lumen
Failure of the urorectal septum to reach the cloacal membrane
Persistence of the entire lumen of the allantois
correctOption: Persistence of a localized area of the allantois with secretory activity
optionExplanations: A urachal cyst occurs when a middle segment of the allantois fails to obliterate, and the secretory lining creates a fluid-filled sac.
Failure of the lateral body wall folds leads to exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, not a localized urachal cyst.
Persistence of the upper part of the lumen forms a urachal sinus, which usually opens at the umbilicus.
Failure of the urorectal septum results in cloacal malformations and rectourinary fistulas, not urachal cysts.
The persistence of the entire lumen results in a urachal fistula, where urine drains from the umbilicus.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): If only a local area of the allantois persists, secretory activity of its lining results in a cystic dilation, a urachal cyst (Fig. 16.15B).

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: At the commencement of the fourth week of human embryonic development, which specific structure represents the initial, vestigial stage of the urinary system in the cervical region?
options: Paramesonephric duct
Pronephros
Metanephric diverticulum
Mesonephric duct
Ureteric bud
correctOption: Pronephros
optionExplanations: The paramesonephric duct is involved in the development of the female genital system and is not part of the initial vestigial cervical excretory system.

The pronephros is the first of three kidney systems. It is nonfunctional, located in the cervical region, and consists of 7-10 cell groups called nephrotomes that disappear by the end of the fourth week.
The metanephric diverticulum, also known as the ureteric bud, appears later in the fifth week and is the precursor to the permanent collecting system, not the initial cervical structure.
The mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct) develops in association with the second kidney system (mesonephros) and extends from the thoracic to the lumbar regions, not restricted to the cervical region.
The ureteric bud is an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct that appears in the fifth week and contributes to the metanephros, which is the third kidney system.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 256 (Book Page): At the beginning of the fourth week, the pronephros is represented by 7 to 10 solid cell groups in the cervical region (Figs. 16.1 and 16.2). These groups form vestigial excretory units, nephrotomes, that regress before more caudal ones are formed.

category: Describe the development of urinary bladder and urethra
statement: A male infant presents with a rare anomaly where the ejaculatory ducts fail to enter the prostatic urethra correctly. Given the embryological development of the urogenital system, which embryological structure's abnormal migration or absorption is most likely responsible for this condition?
options: Urorectal septum
Metanephric mesoderm
Paramesonephric duct
Ureteric bud
Mesonephric duct
correctOption: Mesonephric duct
optionExplanations: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca but does not directly give rise to the ejaculatory ducts.
Metanephric mesoderm gives rise to the excretory units (nephrons) of the kidney, not the ductal system in the pelvis.
Paramesonephric ducts (Mullerian ducts) regress in males due to Anti-Mullerian Hormone and do not form the ejaculatory ducts.
The ureteric bud forms the collecting system of the kidney and the ureter, not the ejaculatory ducts.
The caudal portions of the mesonephric ducts are absorbed into the bladder; in males, the remaining ducts eventually form the ejaculatory ducts entering the prostatic urethra.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 266 (Book Page): those of the mesonephric ducts move close together to enter the prostatic urethra and in the male become the ejaculatory ducts

category: Describe positional changes during descent of kidney with correlation to its blood supply
statement: The definitive kidney (metanephros) begins its function around the 12th week. At this stage, where is the kidney typically located?
options: Attached to the allantois near the umbilicus.
At its near-definitive abdominal level.
Passing through the umbilical arterial fork.
In the pelvic cavity against the sacrum.
Within the thoracic cavity before descending.
correctOption: At its near-definitive abdominal level.
optionExplanations: The bladder is continuous with the allantois via the urachus, but the kidney itself is not attached to the allantois.
As urine production begins (12th week), the kidney has reached its high abdominal position, receiving its supply from the upper lumbar aorta.
The passage through the umbilical fork occurs much earlier during the initial stages of ascent.
By the 12th week, the kidney has already completed most of its ascent from the pelvis.
The kidney never enters the thoracic cavity; its 'ascent' ends in the upper lumbar region.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 263 (Book Page): The kidney, initially in the pelvic region, later shifts to a more cranial position in the abdomen... The definitive kidney formed from the metanephros becomes functional near the 12th week.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: A neonate is born with a flattened face, club feet, and severe respiratory distress. Ultrasound reveals a complete absence of kidneys bilaterally. Which developmental failure is the primary cause of this presentation?
options: Failure of the interaction between the metanephric mesoderm and the ureteric bud
Premature regression of the pronephric nephrotomes in the cervical region
Mutations in genes encoding proteins localized in the primary cilia
Obstruction of the ureteric ascent by the root of the inferior mesenteric artery
Inability of the mesonephric duct to enter the cloaca during the fourth week
correctOption: Failure of the interaction between the metanephric mesoderm and the ureteric bud
optionExplanations: This is correct. Bilateral renal agenesis results in anuria and oligohydramnios, leading to the Potter sequence (flattened facies, club feet, and pulmonary hypoplasia). It is fundamentally a failure of inductive interaction.
Pronephric regression is a normal developmental event and does not lead to renal agenesis or Potter sequence, as the pronephros is never functional.
Ciliary protein mutations are associated with polycystic kidney disease (ciliopathies), not complete renal agenesis. PKD involves the formation of cysts, not the total absence of kidney tissue.
Obstruction by the inferior mesenteric artery results in a horseshoe kidney, not bilateral renal agenesis. Horseshoe kidneys are typically functional despite their abnormal location.

While the ureteric bud originates from the mesonephric duct, bilateral renal agenesis (Potter sequence) is specifically tied to the failure of the bud to form or interact with the metanephric blastema.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 261 (Book Page): Renal agenesis may also arise if the interaction between the metanephric mesoderm and the ureteric bud fails to occur. Normally, during the interaction, GDNF produced by the metanephric mesoderm produces branching and growth of the ureteric bud.

category: Describe the development of pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros
statement: During the formation of the renal pyramid, which embryological event occurs to the collecting tubules of the fifth and successive generations?
options: They acquire a Bowman's capsule from the visceral mesoderm
They elongate considerably and converge on the minor calyx
They degenerate to form the renal sinus
They differentiate into the glomeruli of the outer cortex
They merge to form the ureteric bud
correctOption: They elongate considerably and converge on the minor calyx
optionExplanations: Bowman's capsules are derivatives of the metanephric mesoderm cap, while collecting tubules are derived from the ureteric bud.
The renal pyramids are composed of the straight collecting tubules (from 5th generation onwards) that converge as they drain into the minor calyces.
The renal sinus is a space containing the pelvis and calyces; it is not formed by the degeneration of collecting tubules.
Glomeruli are formed from the metanephric mesoderm (excretory system), not from the collecting tubules of the ureteric bud.
The ureteric bud is the precursor that gives rise to the tubules, not a structure formed by their later merging.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", Page 259 (Book Page): During further development, collecting tubules of the fifth and successive generations elongate considerably and converge on the minor calyx, forming the renal pyramid (Fig. 16.5D).

category: Describe the development of urinary bladder and urethra
statement: The trigone of the urinary bladder has a unique developmental history. What is the initial embryological origin of the mucosa that forms this structure?
options: Metanephric blastema
Urorectal septum mesoderm
Mesonephric duct mesoderm
Genital tubercle ectoderm
Cloacal endoderm
correctOption: Mesonephric duct mesoderm
optionExplanations: The metanephric blastema forms the excretory units (nephrons) of the kidney, not the bladder trigone.
The urorectal septum is mesodermal but its function is to divide the cloaca, not to form the bladder mucosa.
Correct. The trigone is formed by the incorporation of the distal ends of the mesonephric ducts into the bladder wall; since these ducts are mesodermal, the initial trigone lining is mesodermal.
The genital tubercle is involved in the formation of external genitalia, not the internal trigone of the bladder.
While the rest of the bladder is lined with endoderm, the trigone is unique because it is initially formed from the incorporation of mesodermal ducts.
citation: In book "Langman's Medical Embryology", BOOK Page 266 (Book Page): Because both the mesonephric ducts and ureters originate in the mesoderm, the mucosa of the bladder formed by incorporation of the ducts (the trigone of the bladder) is also mesodermal.

Primary budding from the cloaca followed by mesenchyme induction

S-shaped loop formation, glomerular tuft acquisition, and Bowman capsule differentiation
